the prognosis of hypertension declines significantly as the age of onset increases, and that the decline is not explained by any of the known risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
the prognosis of hypertension, as measured by mortality and cardiovascular morbidity rates, declines as age of onset increases from 40 to the late 60s.
the risk of cardiovascular disease in patients with hypertension is related to age at onset of high blood pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the age at onset of high blood pressure and the risk of complications.
the relationship between the risk of cardiovascular disease in hypertension and age at onset of the disease.
the relationship between hypertension and the risk for cardiovascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of cardiovascular events in hypertension increases with age at onset of the hypertension, and this increase in risk is independent of initial blood pressure, control of the hypertension, obesity, alcohol consumption, and smoking.
the risk of hypertension is lower if the disease begins later in life.
the prognosis of hypertension improves as the age at onset increases, at least up to the seventh decade.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of cardiovascular disease in hypertensive subjects is not uniform and is related to the age at which hypertension is diagnosed.
, in the absence of other factors, the prognosis of hypertension is related to age at onset of the condition, but not to the age at which the diagnosis of hypertension is made.
the prognosis of hypertension improves with advancing age at onset of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider the age at onset of a disease when studying the risk of complications, because age of onset can influence the risk even after controlling for other variables.
the risk of cardiovascular morbidity in hypertension declines with age of onset.
it is not the absolute level of blood pressure that matters most, but the level in relation to the age at which it was reached.
